name: The nine obstacles (antarāya), distractions of the mind
description: Illness (vyādhi), dullness (styāna), doubt (saṃśaya), heedlessness (pramāda), laziness (ālasya), non-abstention (avirati), erroneous vision (bhrānti-darśana), failure to gain a stage (alabdha-bhūmikatva) and instability (anavasthitatva): the distractions (vikṣepa) of the mind, which occur together with its activities and are absent when they are absent; Vyāsa also calls them the taints (mala) of yoga, its enemies (pratipakṣa) and obstacles (antarāya) (YS 1.30, YBh 1.30). They do not arise through devotion to Īśvara (YBh 1.29). They are accompanied by pain, dejection, trembling of the limbs and disturbed inhalation and exhalation (YS 1.31).

name: The five accompaniments of distraction (vikṣepa-sahabhuva)
description: Pain (duḥkha, threefold: of oneself, of other beings, of the divine), dejection (daurmanasya: a disturbance of the mind through the frustration of a wish), trembling of the limbs (aṅgamejayatva), inhalation (śvāsa, when the prāṇa takes in outer air) and exhalation (praśvāsa, when it expels air from the belly). Vyāsa: they occur in a distracted mind and do not occur in a concentrated one (YS 1.31, YBh 1.31).

name: The five afflictions (kleśa)
description: Ignorance (avidyā), I-am-ness (asmitā), attachment (rāga), aversion (dveṣa) and clinging to life (abhiniveśa) (YS 2.3); Vyāsa: 'the five errors' (viparyaya), which he names darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom and blind gloom (YBh 1.8). Active, they make firm the office of the guṇas, keep transformation going, raise the stream of cause and effect and, interdependent, bring karma to ripening (YBh 2.3). Ignorance is their field; each is dormant, attenuated, interrupted or fully active, and the burnt-seed state belongs to the last body only (YS 2.4, YBh 2.4). The store of karma is rooted in them (YS 2.12) and ripens while they exist (YS 2.13).

name: Ignorance (avidyā)
description: Taking the impermanent, impure, painful and not-self to be permanent, pure, pleasant and self (YS 2.5). Vyāsa's illustrations: taking the earth, sky and heaven-dwellers to be lasting; taking the body to be pure; taking pain for pleasure; taking the not-self (external instruments, the body, the mind) for self; and rejoicing at the prosperity or grieving at the ruin of what is not the self as if it were one's own. It is a positive contrary cognition, not mere absence of knowledge (like 'non-friend' and 'cow-track'); it is the field of the other four afflictions and the seed of the mass of suffering (YBh 2.4, 2.5, 2.15). Its cause is the latent tendency of erroneous knowledge (YBh 2.24).

name: I-am-ness (asmitā)
description: The seeming identity of the power of the seer (puruṣa) and the power of seeing (buddhi) (YS 2.6). Vyāsa: enjoyment is possible only while the two, utterly distinct, seem undivided; one who does not see the puruṣa as distinct from the buddhi makes a self-notion (ātma-buddhi) there through delusion (YBh 2.6). (Also the name of the fourth samādhi accompaniment, YS 1.17.)

name: Harmful thoughts (vitarka): violence and the rest
description: Thoughts of violence and the rest (untruth, stealing, unchastity, possessiveness), whether done, caused to be done or approved, preceded by greed, anger or delusion, mild, middling or intense, with unending suffering and ignorance as fruit (YS 2.34). Vyāsa's own description of how they show themselves: 'I will kill the one who wronged me; I will tell a lie; I will take his goods; I will lie with his wives; I will become owner of his possessions' — the 'fever of thoughts' (vitarka-jvara) that inflames the mind and draws it toward the wrong road (YBh 2.33). Vyāsa counts twenty-seven forms of violence, then eighty-one, then countless (YBh 2.34).

name: Gross and subtle activities of the afflictions
description: The gross activities of the afflictions are thinned by kriyā-yoga and abandoned by meditation as discerning insight; the subtle ones (seeds) are abandoned by involution (pratiprasava). As gross dirt is shaken from cloth first and fine dirt removed later with effort, the gross activities have small opposition and the subtle ones great (YS 2.10–2.11, YBh 2.11).
